title: The winter solstice
hookLine: the longest night, and the light returns from here

cards: Four-thirty in the afternoon and it's already dark. You leave work in the dark; you might have arrived in it too. In the far north, the sun barely clears the horizon, or doesn't rise at all.
And yet, all around the world, this darkest stretch of the year is full of lights. Strings of them on houses. Candles in windows.

In Iran, families stay up through Yalda, the longest night, eating pomegranates and reading poetry. Other traditions keep their own festivals of light around now, each with its own meaning. Today: the winter solstice.

teach.h: THE LONGEST NIGHT IS ALSO THE TURN.
teach.b: First, the turn at the bottom. At the summer solstice, the peak of the light was also the start of its going. Now it's the mirror: the longest night is the moment the light starts coming back.
Tomorrow will be a little longer than today, though nobody will notice at first. Second, Seneca on the seasons. In one letter he tells Lucilius that the world itself runs on change.
Winter brings the cold, and we have to shiver. Summer brings the heat, and we have to sweat.

We can't change that order, he says, but we can take on a great spirit, worthy of a good person, and bear what comes bravely, in agreement with nature. The dark isn't a punishment. It's part of the turning.
Third, a Stoic and his lamp. Epictetus tells his students he once had an iron lamp by his household gods, and a thief stole it. Tomorrow, he says, I'll buy a clay one.
And the thief paid a higher price: to get the lamp, he agreed to become a thief. A lamp can be replaced. What Epictetus chooses to be cannot be stolen.
Fourth, why a candle. A candle in the dark doesn't argue with the night or make it day.
It just makes a small circle where you can see a face, a page, your own hands.
Getting through a hard season often looks like that: not ending the dark, but keeping one small light going until the days lengthen on their own.

how: Several traditions hold festivals of light around the winter solstice, each with its own meaning; some people mark the longest night simply by lighting a candle and keeping company.

practice: Light a candle safely, or turn on one small lamp and turn the others off, and notice how far the light reaches and where the dark begins. Don't push the dark away; let the small light be enough.
Then hold in mind one person who's in a dark season right now, inside this small circle of light.

wordCard.voice: Winter solstice, the longest night of the year, and the turning point after which the light returns, little by little. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the light returns. Little by little, whether anyone notices or not. Day six hundred seventy-three.
